The Maharashtra State Council of Educational Research and Training was established in Pune in 1984, and it brings out the periodical Jeevan Shikshan. Balbharati publishes Kishor, a monthly magazine for children, so option (a) is not correct, and the University Education Commission was a body appointed for higher education and not the publisher of this magazine.

[Note: the chapter supplies only these facts about the NCERT. It does not give the further information that the question asks the student to obtain from the internet, such as the Council's later milestones, any changes in its structure, or the names of its office-bearers.]

The Census figures showed that literacy in the country was still low, for it had risen only to 52 per cent by 1991, and improving this percentage was a serious challenge for the government of India. Even after Operation Blackboard was started in 1988, primary education had still not reached every child, so a programme aimed directly at making primary education universal was needed. For this reason the District Primary Education Programme was started in 1994 and was implemented in seven States, including Maharashtra. It was undertaken because attendance in primary schools had to be raised to 100 per cent, the dropping out of students had to be arrested, and education had to reach girls and physically handicapped children. To achieve these aims the programme included research on and evaluation of primary education, alternative education and the creation of awareness in society.

The Central Government needed a body of its own to help it in matters of school education in the context of a comprehensive policy and in implementing its educational schemes. For this reason the National Council of Educational Research and Training was established in Delhi on 1 September 1961. It was established because the country needed one agency to take up educational research and development, training, extension, educational programmes and the restructuring of school curriculum and textbooks. Since its establishment it has played a central role in designing school curricula and textbooks with the cooperation of the Central Board of Secondary Education, has guided the State governments in primary and secondary education, has prepared workbooks and handbooks for teachers and has conducted talent search examinations at the national level.

The Indian Agricultural Research Institute was given the status of a University in 1958, after which work began in departments such as development of the agriculture sector, research, well-equipped laboratories, soil science, agricultural sciences and economic botany. Research was taken up on wheat, pulses, oilseeds, vegetables and many other problems, that is, on the very crops and difficulties that a farmer has to deal with. Its most significant achievement is the fundamental research it conducted on the methods of taking multiple crops in a year, and because a farmer can now take more than one crop from the same land in a year, this work has been of great benefit to farmers. The Institute also maintains at its head office in Delhi the biggest agriculture-related library in the country, so that this knowledge remains available for further use.

The Indira Gandhi National Open University was established with the objective that the stream of education should make its way into every average household of the country. The United Nations declared 1970 the International Education Year, and in the same year a seminar on the Open University was organised in New Delhi by the Government of India Departments of Education and Social Welfare and of Information and Broadcasting and by the University Grants Commission along with UNESCO; the idea of establishing an open university evolved in this seminar. In 1974 the government appointed a committee under the chairmanship of P. Parthasarathy, and in accordance with its recommendations the Open University took shape on 20 September 1985 and was named after Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Those who are unable to get a college education in the formal way are given concessions in the eligibility criteria, in age and in other conditions for admission to this university. In 1990 the IGNOU started an audio-visual distance education programme through Akashvani and Doordarshan, and it has conducted more than one thousand curricula of various branches through 58 training centres in the country and 41 centres in foreign countries.

In 1964 a Commission was appointed under the chairmanship of Dr D. S. Kothari, and Dr J. P. Naik made valuable contributions to its work. The Commission recommended the 10+2+3 pattern for secondary, higher secondary and university education, and this system was implemented from 1972. It also suggested a uniform national system of education, the inclusion of the mother tongue, Hindi and English in education, and continuing education, adult education, education by correspondence and open universities, so that education would trickle down to the lowest rungs of society. It further recommended increased provision in the government's budget for expenditure on the education of neglected sections such as the scheduled castes and tribes. The Maharashtra government adopted the 10+2+3 pattern in 1972 and conducted its first Std X Board examination in 1975.

The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre has conducted valuable research in the fields of nuclear physics, solid state physics, spectroscopy and the chemical and life sciences. It also started a school to train scientists for setting up nuclear reactors, so that the country would have its own trained scientists for this work.
[Note: the chapter does not state when or where the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre was established, or by whom, so those details are not given here.]

The Maharashtra State Bureau of Textbook Production and Curriculum Research, which is known as Balbharati, was established in Pune on 27 January 1967. Balbharati prepares the textbooks for school children of the 1st to the 12th standards. These textbooks are made in eight languages, namely Marathi, Hindi, English, Urdu, Kannad, Sindhi, Gujarati and Telugu. Balbharati also publishes Kishor, a monthly magazine for children.

Operation Blackboard was the scheme started by the central government in 1988 for the spread of primary education and to improve educational standards. Under it the government made funds available to help improve the standard of the schools and to fulfil their minimum educational needs. These needs included at least two proper classrooms and toilets, and two teachers of whom one was to be a woman. Every school was also to have a blackboard, maps, laboratory apparatus, a small library, a playground and sports equipment. In 1994 the scheme was expanded, and provision was made for one additional classroom and for appointing one more teacher in schools with an enrolment of more than 100 students. In this expansion priority was given to girls' schools, to schools with a majority of scheduled caste and scheduled tribe students and to schools in rural areas. It was also made binding upon the State government to appoint female teachers to fifty per cent of the posts in schools. Through these programmes the scheme helped the primary education system to gain some momentum.

Institutions that teach and research agriculture carry the science of farming to the farmer, and in India this work is best seen in the Indian Agricultural Research Institute. Research in agriculture had begun in India as early as 1905, and in 1958 the Indian Agricultural Research Institute was given the status of a University. Work then began in departments such as development of the agriculture sector, research, well-equipped laboratories, soil science, agricultural sciences and economic botany. Research was also taken up on wheat, pulses, oilseeds, vegetables and many other problems. Its most significant achievement is the fundamental research it conducted on the methods of taking multiple crops in a year, which has been of great benefit to farmers. The Institute maintains at its head office in Delhi the biggest agriculture-related library in the country, so that the knowledge it gathers is available to all who study agriculture. In these ways such an institution improves crops, prepares trained people for the agriculture sector and passes new methods on to the farmer, and so helps agriculture to develop.
[Note: the chapter describes only the Indian Agricultural Research Institute. It does not separately describe agriculture schools or colleges or the courses they teach, so this answer is based on the work of that Institute.]

India has made steady progress in medical research, medical education and treatment since Independence. In 1949 the Indian Council for Medical Research was established for conducting research in the medical field, and it was given the responsibility of cooperating with universities, medical colleges and government and non-government research institutes and of giving them guidance and financial support. Twenty-six centres were started in different parts of the country for research on various diseases, and their research has made it possible to control tuberculosis and leprosy. The All India Institute of Medical Sciences was established to give further impetus to advanced education and research in medicine, and it was given the responsibility of undergraduate and postgraduate courses in most branches of medicine, with good research facilities and well-equipped hospitals. The AIIMS also provides medical treatment to the common people at nominal rates, and it has established special colleges for training in nursing and super-speciality centres for the treatment of disorders of the heart, brain and eyes. For the further development of the medical field, the Medical Council of India was restructured in 1958 and was entrusted with determining the criteria for the quality of medical education and with its supervision and inspection. In the field of cancer, the Advanced Centre for Treatment, Research and Education in Cancer, which is a branch of the Tata Memorial Centre, functions as the national centre for treatment, research and education in relation to cancer. The Indian systems of medicine were not neglected, for the Central Council for Research in Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy was established in 1969, and in 1979 it was replaced by three separate councils for research in Unani Medicine, in Homoeopathy and in Yoga and Nature Cure. The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research added to this progress by preparing medicines for malaria, elephantiasis and tuberculosis.

Curricular activities are the activities of the regular curriculum, that is, the daily teaching of subjects such as the languages, mathematics, science and the social sciences, the practical work that goes with them, and the class tests and school examinations. In our school these subjects are taught with the help of a blackboard, maps and laboratory apparatus, and the school library is used for reading and reference; these are the very facilities that the Operation Blackboard scheme wanted every school to have. Co-curricular activities are the activities conducted alongside the curriculum to develop the other abilities of a pupil. Sports and games are held on the school playground with the school's sports equipment, and drawing is encouraged through the drawing grade examinations that are organised at the school level. Cultural programmes, elocution and essay competitions and the celebration of days of national importance teach pupils to speak well and to work together. A science exhibition is also organised, in which pupils prepare models and activities on subjects such as water purification and explain them to the visitors. Educational visits, tree plantation and cleanliness drives take pupils outside the classroom and teach them by doing, the method that Tarabai Modak worked hard to bring into education. Taken together, the curricular activities give a pupil knowledge and the co-curricular activities give health, skill, confidence and good habits, and both are needed for a complete education.
[Note: the chapter does not describe any particular school. This answer is a model, and each student should change it to match the activities that are actually conducted in his or her own school.]
